Chapter 11: Natural Rights, Section 1: Life, Subsection: Guns

“Stop quoting laws, we carry weapons!” ~ Pompey the Great, Roman general & politician; Life of Pompey

The right to life necessarily means the right to the protection of said life–the right to ensure that the life continues. The most effective way to protect oneself is a form of defense, and today that means owning a gun. The United States, being a nation which was founded on the principles of natural rights, enshrines the private ownership of arms in its Constitution–a document which today has been illegally–treasonously–foregone by the government.

“A well-regulated militia being necessary to the security of a free state, the right of the people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed.” ~ Second Amendment to the United States Constitution

“Ah, but what does that have to do with private gun ownership? I see the word ‘militia’ in there. That means the military.”

Time for a crash course in what the Second Amendment really means and how it has been violated throughout history. Word by word:

Well-Regulated. The following is taken from the Oxford English Dictionary, and from social understanding at the time of the writing of the Second Amendment.

  • 1709: If a liberal education has formed in us well-regulated appetites and worthy inclinations.
  • 1714: The practice of all well-regulated courts of justice in the world.
  • 1812: The equation of time is the adjustment of the difference of time as shown by a well-regulated clock and a true sundial.
  • 1848: A remissness for which I am sure every well-regulated person will blame the Mayor.
  • 1862: It appeared to her well-regulated mind, like a clandestine proceeding.
  • 1894: The newspaper, a never wanting adjunct to every well-regulated American embryo city.

The phrase ‘well-regulated’ was in common use long before 1789 and remained so for a century thereafter. It referred to the act of something being in proper working order. Something “well-regulated” is calibrated correctly and functioning as expected. Establishing government oversight of the people’s arms was not the intent of using the phrase in the Second Amendment. The founders wrote it precisely to render the government powerless to do so.

“By calling attention to ‘a well regulated militia,’ the ‘security’ of the nation, and the right of each citizen ‘to keep and bear arms,’ our Founding Fathers recognized the essentially civilian nature of our economy. Although it is extremely unlikely that the fears of governmental tyranny which gave rise to the Second Amendment will ever be a major danger to our nation, the Amendment still remains an important declaration of our basic civilian-military relationships, in which every citizen must be ready to participate in the defense of his country. For that reason I believe the Second Amendment will always be important.” ~ John F. Kennedy; Know Your Lawmakers, p. 4

Militia. Militia refers to the entire pool of citizens capable of military service. It is sometimes claimed that the National Guard “replaced” the militia. This is clearly shown to be false by 10 U.S. Code § 311 and the Militia Act of 1903. This act clarified that the National Guard is an organized militia and all able-bodied men, ages 17-45, were part of the reserve militia. The Militia Act of 1903 repealed the Militia Act of 1792, which had simply required all able-bodied men to provide their own firearm.

To Keep And Bear. To keep means to have. To bear, in this context, means to carry or hold. The phrase, very simply, means that you may not only own firearms, you may carry them on your person. The government cannot stop you.

Shall Not Be Infringed. The last part acts on the previous phrase, “to keep and to bear.” Infringe means to wrongly limit or restrict.

Written in more modern terms, the Second Amendment might read something like this: A properly armed people is necessary for a state to be free and secure. People can own and carry any weapon, and the government can’t do anything about it. Since that’s not enough for some folks, let’s head back to high school and do some sentence diagramming.

It is a compound sentence composed of two clauses. What is the well-regulated militia doing? –> being necessary. What is the right of the people to keep and bear arms doing? –> not being infringed at a future date (conjugated form of “to be”: “shall”). Is the subject of the first clause related to the predicate of the second clause? –> No. Who has an uninfringeable right to keep and bear arms: the people or the militia? –> The people. Does the militia matter at all in the context of the right guaranteed by this sentence? –> No. Its existence is merely stated to be a necessity for a free state’s security. The right of the people to keep and bear arms exists independently of the militia; however, the militia cannot exist independent of a right of the people to keep and bear arms. This is why it was mentioned in the amendment.

Another example: “A well-balanced breakfast being necessary to the start of a healthy day, the right of the people to keep and eat food shall not be infringed.” Who has the right to keep and eat food: ‘a breakfast’ or ‘the people’? This is being repeated in such detail because of its direct import to every other topic mentioned in this book. If the government can steal your means of protecting your life, they have stolen your life itself. Inequality of arms between the state and the people was responsible for the majority of human history being characterized by authoritarian monarchies such as kingdoms and empires. Over 90% of the populace was powerless serfs or peasants, tied to the land. Taxes were extorted from them by force. They were held in check by the well-equipped and well-armed nobleman’s forces. Swords and armor were extremely expensive–and effective, in an age without crossbows and guns. Crossbows could shoot through the strongest of plate armor and allowed a peasant trained in about a day to be able to resist a knight trained from childhood. Is it any wonder that the Magna Carta, signed in 1215, coincided with the rise of crossbows? Or that the Catholic church wanted to ban crossbows in Europe for being too deadly?

Then firearms and the gunpowder revolution changed military tactics forever. It wasn’t until the latter half of the 18th century that the mass production of firearms allowed everyone to afford a rifle. This equality of arms between the people and the state allowed for individuals to assert their natural rights such as speech, thought, property ownership, and self defense. That is why all the North and South American revolutions occurred when they did–because the people finally had power to resist the state. The military technology possessed by the state was equal to that of the people. But we now seeing again a rise in the inequality of arms between the people and the state, not the least of which because the government is illegally restricting the right to keep and bear arms.

“It is unfortunately true that the great body of our citizens shoot less and less as time goes on. To meet this, we should encourage rifle practice among schoolboys, and indeed among all classes, as well as in the military services, by every means in our power. Thus, and not otherwise, may we be able to assist in preserving the peace of the world. Fit to hold our own against the strong nations of the earth, our voice for peace will carry to the ends of the earth. “Okay, the Constitution says the people can have guns and the government can’t stop them. What does that have to do with the right to life? Guns kill!”

Additionally, only you have the right to the defense of your life. If you aren’t allowed to protect your own life, how can anyone else have that responsibility? What value does your life have if it isn’t worth defending? Is innocent life valuable?

“Yes, of course.”

Is innocent life worth protecting?

Should people, then, be allowed to effectively defend themselves?
